classification.habitat: Dry scrub, riverbanks, roadsides and open woodland
classification.distribution: Widespread in the Indian subcontinent and other tropical Asian regions

identification.description: Aromatic shrub with opposite palmately compound leaves, commonly with five leaflets, and small bluish-purple flowers.
identification.whole_plant: Much-branched aromatic shrub or small tree.
identification.root: Woody branched root system; crude root should be authenticated.
identification.stem: Young branches quadrangular to subquadrangular; older stems woody.
identification.leaf: Opposite, palmately compound, usually 3–5 narrow lanceolate leaflets; aromatic when crushed.
identification.flower: Small bluish-purple to violet flowers in terminal or axillary panicles/spikes.
identification.fruit: Small globose drupe, darkening as it matures.
identification.seed: Single-seeded drupe containing a hard seed-like endocarp.

therapeutics.precautions: Use authenticated plant material; topical and internal use should follow appropriate references.

modern_information.evidence_summary: Vitex negundo has been investigated for anti-inflammatory and analgesic-related pharmacological activity; this record does not convert experimental findings into clinical efficacy claims.
modern_information.safety_notes: Avoid relying on unverified preparations; consider interactions and pregnancy-related clinical considerations when relevant.

exam_points: Leaf usually palmately compound with 3–5 leaflets
Leaf is a commonly used part
student.quick_revision: Nirgundi (Vitex negundo): aromatic shrub of Lamiaceae with opposite palmately compound leaves and bluish-purple flowers; leaf is an important useful part.

teaching_points: Demonstrate palmately compound leaf and aromatic odour.
Discuss botanical authentication of Vitex species.
discussion_points: Traditional Vata/Shotha profile and modern pharmacological research
practical_points: Count leaflets and inspect their arrangement.
Observe flower colour and fruiting drupes.

doctor.quick_reference: Nirgundi is traditionally used in Vata- and Shotha-related contexts; dosing requires a verified classical/pharmacopoeial source.
key_precautions: Do not infer dose from this educational record
